claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
The untreated alloy exhibits brittle failure during room-temperature tensile loading.
Dislocation pile-ups occur at internal phase boundaries in the untreated alloy.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries produce local stress concentrations.
The local stress concentrations promote microcracking and catastrophic failure.
A targeted surface treatment or interface-specific nanoscale coating can selectively segregate ductility-enhancing elements to internal phase boundaries.
Controlled interfacial chemical modification will create ductile complexions at internal phase boundaries.
The resulting ductile interfacial regions will facilitate smoother dislocation transmission across phase boundaries.
Smoother dislocation transmission will reduce dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries.
Reducing dislocation pile-ups will lower local stress concentrations.
Lower interfacial stress concentrations will mitigate microcracking and delay catastrophic failure.
The treatment will increase room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will maintain or slightly increase tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Insufficient treatment depth or nonuniform segregation would limit modification of critical internal boundaries and reduce treatment effectiveness.
Adverse changes in phase compatibility could limit the effectiveness of the treatment.
